changes.old: Narsai founded a new school at Nisibis in Persian lands, and most of the students from the school of Edessa came to him.
changes.new: Narsai founded a new school at Nisibis in Persian lands, and most of the students from the school of Edessa came to him.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: An imperial law of July 381 forbade Eunomians to build churches in town or country and seized any land where they did.
changes.new: An imperial law of July 381 forbade Eunomians to build churches in town or country. It seized any land where they did.
changes.facts_check: Imperial law, July 381; Eunomians forbidden to build churches in town or country; land seized; split only (old FK 10.02); all kept.

changes.old: The bishops whom Theodosius gathered at Constantinople anathematized the Semi-Arians, also called Pneumatomachi, in their first canon.
changes.new: Theodosius had the bishops meet at Constantinople. In their first canon they put a curse on the Semi-Arians, who were also known as the Pneumatomachi.
changes.facts_check: Bishops gathered by Theodosius at Constantinople; first canon; anathema (curse) on Semi-Arians alias Pneumatomachi; all kept.

changes.old: A law of March 388 drove the Apollinarians from the cities and stripped their bishops of the title of bishop.
changes.new: A law of March 388 drove the Apollinarians from the cities and stripped their bishops of the title of bishop.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: The bishops of Gaul refused communion to Saturninus and condemned the creed sent to them from Sirmium as soon as it arrived.
changes.new: The bishops of Gaul refused communion to Saturninus. They condemned the creed sent to them from Sirmium as soon as it came.
changes.facts_check: Gallic bishops; communion refused to Saturninus; Sirmium creed condemned on arrival; all kept.

changes.old: An imperial law of July 383 banned Arians, along with Eunomians and other groups, from meeting or gathering any crowd.
changes.new: In July 383 an imperial law said the Arians could not meet or gather any crowd. Eunomians and other groups were banned as well.
changes.facts_check: Imperial law, July 383; Arians barred from meeting or gathering crowds; Eunomians and other groups included; all kept.

changes.old: A council of nineteen bishops at Rome, granted by Constantine, condemned Donatus and cleared his rival Caecilian.
changes.new: Constantine gave leave for a council of nineteen bishops to meet at Rome. It found Donatus guilty and cleared his rival, Caecilian.
changes.facts_check: Council of nineteen bishops at Rome granted by Constantine; Donatus condemned (verdict); Caecilian cleared; all kept.

changes.old: In a canon, the Persian bishops bound themselves to serve the liturgy by the western order that Bishops Isaac and Marutha had taught them.
changes.new: In a canon, the Persian bishops made a pledge. They would serve the liturgy in the western way that Bishops Isaac and Marutha had taught them.
changes.facts_check: Canon; Persian bishops bind themselves; liturgy by western order taught by Isaac and Marutha; all kept.

changes.old: The Council in Trullo at Constantinople set its seal on the canons of Gregory the Wonderworker, alongside those of the great councils.
changes.new: At Constantinople, the Council in Trullo set its seal on the canons of Gregory the Wonderworker. It put them with those of the great councils.
changes.facts_check: Council in Trullo, Constantinople; confirms Gregory the Wonderworker's canons alongside great councils'; all kept.

changes.old: Meetings of the faithful across Asia judged the New Prophecy heretical, and its followers were expelled from the church and barred from communion.
changes.new: Meetings of the faithful across Asia judged the New Prophecy to be heresy. Its followers were thrown out of the church and barred from communion.
changes.facts_check: Asian meetings of the faithful; New Prophecy judged heretical; followers expelled and debarred from communion; all kept.

changes.old: Constantine's law banned Montanist meetings even in private houses and urged them to join the catholic Church instead.
changes.new: Constantine's law said the Montanists could not meet, not even in a private house. It urged them to join the catholic Church instead.
changes.facts_check: Constantine's law; Montanist meetings banned incl. private houses; urged to enter catholic Church; all kept.

changes.old: Justinian ordered the Montanists to give up their faith, Procopius says, and threatened holdouts with losing the right to leave property to their families.
changes.new: Justinian ordered the Montanists to give up their faith, Procopius says. He threatened those who held out with losing the right to leave property to their families.
changes.facts_check: Justinian; Montanists ordered to abandon faith; Procopius attribution kept; recusants threatened with loss of right to bequeath to family; all kept.

changes.old: The Council of Nicaea let Novatianist clergy keep their rank if they promised in writing to follow the teaching of the Catholic Church.
changes.new: The Council of Nicaea let Novatianist clergy keep their rank. First they had to promise in writing to follow the teaching of the Catholic Church.
changes.facts_check: Nicaea; Novatianist clergy keep rank on written promise to follow Catholic teaching; condition kept as prerequisite.

changes.old: The church later threw Marcion out, Tertullian says, and turned away the money he had given it along with him.
changes.new: The church later threw Marcion out, Tertullian says, and turned away the money he had given it along with him.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: The church at Rome expelled Valentinus more than once, Tertullian says, for spreading his ideas among its members.
changes.new: Tertullian says the church at Rome threw out Valentinus more than once for spreading his ideas among its members.
changes.facts_check: Tertullian attribution; Rome church expelled Valentinus more than once; cause (infecting the brethren) kept.

changes.old: The meetings at Antioch over Paul of Samosata, which Gregory and Athenodorus joined, ended when a final synod excommunicated him.
changes.new: Gregory and Athenodorus took part in the meetings at Antioch on Paul of Samosata. These came to an end when a last synod cut him off from communion.
changes.facts_check: Meetings at Antioch over Paul of Samosata; Gregory and Athenodorus joined; ended with final synod excommunicating him; all kept.

changes.old: A law of July 381 ordered every church handed to bishops in communion with Helladius of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa, among others.
changes.new: A law of July 381 named Helladius of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa and others. It said all churches must go to bishops in communion with them.
changes.facts_check: Law of July 381; every church to bishops in communion with Helladius of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa and others the law names; all kept.

changes.old: Ambrose won a promise from Theodosius to amend his edict on the burned synagogue and to end the whole investigation.
changes.new: Ambrose got Theodosius to promise two things. He would change his edict on the burned synagogue, and he would end the whole inquiry.
changes.facts_check: Ambrose obtains Theodosius's promise to amend the synagogue edict and end the whole investigation; all kept.

changes.old: A law of July 381 ordered every church handed to bishops in communion with Diodore of Tarsus and others it named.
changes.new: A law of July 381 named Diodore of Tarsus and others. It said that every church must go to bishops in communion with them.
changes.facts_check: Law of July 381; every church to bishops in communion with Diodore of Tarsus and others it named; all kept.

changes.old: After synods condemned John Chrysostom, his followers, called Johannites, left the church and held their own assemblies apart.
changes.new: After synods condemned John Chrysostom, his followers left the church. They met on their own and were known as the Johannites.
changes.facts_check: Synods condemned Chrysostom; followers separated, held assemblies apart, called Johannites; all kept.

changes.old: The Second Council of Constantinople cursed Theodore of Mopsuestia and all who defended him or called his reading of Scripture orthodox.
changes.new: The Second Council of Constantinople cursed Theodore of Mopsuestia. It also cursed all who stood up for him or said the way he read Scripture was orthodox.
changes.facts_check: Constantinople II anathematizes Theodore and those who defend him or call his exegesis orthodox; all kept.

changes.old: At Aquileia the bishops condemned Palladius, judged him unworthy of the priesthood and ordered a Catholic bishop ordained in his place.
changes.new: At Aquileia the bishops condemned Palladius. They found him unworthy to be a priest, and said a Catholic must be made bishop in his place.
changes.facts_check: Aquileia; Palladius condemned, judged unworthy of priesthood, Catholic to be ordained bishop in his place; all kept.

changes.old: The Council of Trent declared the old Latin Vulgate the authentic text for public lectures, debates, sermons and expositions, and let no one reject it.
changes.new: The Council of Trent made the old Latin Vulgate the authentic text for public lectures, debates, sermons and teaching. No one could reject it.
changes.facts_check: Trent; old Vulgate held authentic for lectures, disputations, sermons, expositions ("teaching"); no one to reject it; all kept.

changes.old: Justinian forbade Donatists, Arians, Jews and pagans to keep meeting places or hold rites in the manner of the church.
changes.new: Justinian banned Donatists, Arians, Jews and pagans from having places to meet. Nor could they hold rites as the church does.
changes.facts_check: Justinian; Donatists, Arians, Jews, pagans; no meeting places, no rites quasi ritu ecclesiastico; all kept.

changes.old: Once the case was reported to the palace, the emperor decreed that Priscillian and his friends be put to death.
changes.new: Once the case was reported to the palace, the emperor decreed that Priscillian and his friends be put to death.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: On Severus's advice, Dioscorus of Alexandria won back men who had long refused communion, and they joined the Egyptian church.
changes.new: Dioscorus of Alexandria took Severus's advice. He won back men who had long kept out of communion, and they joined the Egyptian church.
changes.facts_check: On Severus's advice Dioscorus won back long-separated men, who joined the Egyptian church; all kept.

changes.old: Reparatus of Carthage lost his office and was sent into exile for refusing to condemn the Three Chapters, and his own envoy was made bishop in his place.
changes.new: Reparatus of Carthage would not condemn the Three Chapters. For this he lost his office and was exiled, and his own envoy was made bishop in his place.
changes.facts_check: Reparatus refused to condemn Three Chapters; deprived of office, exiled; his apocrisiarius made bishop; all kept.

changes.old: Justinian's law ordered every copy of Severus's writings burned and barred him from the capital and its district.
changes.new: Justinian's law said every copy of Severus's writings must be burned. It also kept him out of the capital and the land around it.
changes.facts_check: Justinian's law; Severus's writings burned; barred from capital and its district; all kept.

changes.old: A synod at Dvin in 554, under Catholicos Nerses II, confirmed the Armenian church's refusal of Chalcedon and proclaimed the faith of Ephesus against it.
changes.new: In 554 Catholicos Nerses II held a synod at Dvin. It confirmed that the Armenian church would not accept Chalcedon, and set out the faith of Ephesus against it.
changes.facts_check: Dvin 554 under Nerses II; confirmed refusal of Chalcedon; proclaimed Ephesus faith against it; all kept.

changes.old: Nerses Bakur, head of the Albanian church, was removed for leaning toward communion with the Greek church, and Simeon took his place.
changes.new: Nerses Bakur, head of the Albanian church, leaned toward communion with the Greek church. For this he was removed, and Simeon took his place.
changes.facts_check: Nerses Bakur, Albanian head; inclined to Greek communion; removed; replaced by Simeon; all kept.

changes.old: In 802 Charlemagne ordered that whatever monasteries did against the Rule of Saint Benedict be put right by that rule.
changes.new: In 802 Charlemagne gave an order about monasteries. Anything done in them against the Rule of Saint Benedict was to be put right by that rule.
changes.facts_check: 802; Charlemagne; whatever monasteries did against Benedict's Rule to be corrected by that rule; all kept.

changes.old: Justinian barred every Christian outside the orthodox faith from baptism and the other sacraments, and Arian soldiers in the Roman army joined a mutiny over it.
changes.new: Justinian let no Christian outside the orthodox faith have baptism or any other rite of the church. Arian soldiers in the Roman army took part in a mutiny over it.
changes.facts_check: Justinian barred non-orthodox Christians from baptism and other sacraments ("rite of the church"); Arian soldiers joined mutiny; all kept.

changes.old: In 589 the third council of Toledo cursed anyone who still held to the faith and communion that came from Arius.
changes.new: In 589 the third council of Toledo cursed anyone who still held to the faith and communion that came from Arius.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: In 664 the king and all present at the debate resolved to follow the Catholic Easter, and Bishop Colman went back to Scotland with those who would not.
changes.new: In 664 the king and all at the debate decided to follow the Catholic Easter. Bishop Colman went back to Scotland with those who would not.
changes.facts_check: 664; king and all present resolved for Catholic Easter; Colman returned to Scotland with dissenters; all kept.

changes.old: In 742 Carloman, advised by Boniface and his fellow bishops, ordered a church synod every year to restore church law and correct Christian practice.
changes.new: In 742 Carloman, on the advice of Boniface and his fellow bishops, ordered a church synod each year. Its aim was to restore church law and correct Christian practice.
changes.facts_check: 742; Carloman advised by Boniface and bishops; annual synod to restore church law and amend Christian practice; all kept.

changes.old: The iconoclast council of 754 declared John of Damascus deposed and cursed, along with Germanus of Constantinople and George.
changes.new: In 754 a council against icons said John of Damascus was deposed and cursed. It said the same of George and of Germanus of Constantinople.
changes.facts_check: Iconoclast council 754 declared John of Damascus, Germanus of Constantinople and George deposed and anathematized; all kept.

changes.old: At the Second Council of Nicaea, bishops who had opposed images read confessions venerating them, and the synod received them back.
changes.new: At the Second Council of Nicaea, bishops who had been against images read out confessions that venerated them. The synod then took them back.
changes.facts_check: Nicaea II; formerly iconoclast bishops read confessions venerating images and were received back; all kept.

changes.old: The patriarch Theodosius made a church law binding the metropolitans of India, China and other far lands to send letters of communion every six years.
changes.new: The patriarch Theodosius made a church law. It bound the metropolitans of India, China and other far lands to send letters of communion every six years.
changes.facts_check: Patriarch Theodosius; canon binding metropolitans of India, China, far lands to send communion letters every six years (as before); all kept.

changes.old: At the Carmelites' request in 1247, Pope Innocent IV confirmed a corrected and softened version of their rule.
changes.new: In 1247 the Carmelites asked Pope Innocent IV to confirm their rule in a form that had been corrected and softened. He did so.
changes.facts_check: 1247; at Carmelites' request Innocent IV confirmed the corrected and mitigated rule; all kept.

changes.old: Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, gave the Carmelite friars their rule, which their order later asked the pope to explain, correct and soften.
changes.new: Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, gave the Carmelite friars their rule. Later the friars asked the pope to explain, correct and soften it.
changes.facts_check: Albert of Jerusalem gave the rule; order later asked pope to explain, correct, mitigate; all kept.

changes.old: Pope Innocent III granted and confirmed Francis's way of life for him and for all his brothers, present and future.
changes.new: Pope Innocent III granted and confirmed Francis's way of life for him and for all his brothers, present and future.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: The Council of Vienne formally condemned eight errors that it charged to the beguines and beghards of Germany.
changes.new: The Council of Vienne formally condemned eight errors. It said they were held by the beguines and beghards of Germany.
changes.facts_check: Vienne; eight errors formally condemned; charged to German beguines and beghards; all kept.

changes.old: The Council of Vienne in 1311-12 ruled as error the claim that those who live in the spirit of liberty owe no human obedience.
changes.new: The Council of Vienne in 1311-12 ruled as error the claim that those who live in the spirit of liberty owe no human obedience.
changes.facts_check: Already passes; unchanged.

changes.old: Pope Pius V abolished the order of Humiliati brothers, along with its general, its provincial heads and all its statutes.
changes.new: Pope Pius V put an end to the order of Humiliati brothers. He also did away with its general, its heads in each province and all its statutes.
changes.facts_check: Pius V abolished Humiliati order with its general, provincials and all statutes; all kept.

changes.old: Pope Innocent III approved the Humiliati in 1200, and the order soon grew to 220 houses in the province of Milan alone.
changes.new: In 1200 Pope Innocent III approved the Humiliati. They soon had 220 houses in just the province of Milan.
changes.facts_check: 1200 approval by Innocent III; soon 220 houses in Milan province alone; all kept.

changes.old: A church council at Rome, held before the Lateran council, judged Valdes's followers schismatics and then condemned them as heretics.
changes.new: A church council at Rome met before the Lateran one. It judged Valdes's followers guilty of schism, and then it condemned them as heretics.
changes.facts_check: Roman council before Lateran; Valdes's followers judged schismatics, then condemned as heretics; all kept.

changes.old: In 1179 the Third Lateran Council cut off the Cathars and all who defended or sheltered them, and barred anyone from housing them.
changes.new: In 1179 the Third Lateran Council cut off the Cathars and all who defended or sheltered them. It barred anyone from housing them.
changes.facts_check: 1179 Lateran III; anathema on Cathars, defenders and receivers; ban on housing them; all kept.

changes.old: Emperor Alexios I had the Bogomil leader Basil burned in the Hippodrome and kept his many followers in prison until they died.
changes.new: Emperor Alexios I had Basil, who led the Bogomils, burned in the Hippodrome. He kept the many who followed Basil in jail till they died.
changes.facts_check: Alexios I; Bogomil leader Basil burned in Hippodrome; his many followers imprisoned until death; all kept.

changes.old: The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 condemned and rejected the treatise Joachim wrote against Peter Lombard on the Trinity.
changes.new: In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council condemned and rejected a book by Joachim. In it he wrote against Peter Lombard on the Trinity.
changes.facts_check: 1215 Lateran IV; condemned and rejected Joachim's treatise (libellum) against Peter Lombard on the Trinity; all kept.

changes.old: In 1312 Pope Clement V, with the Council of Vienne's approval, did away with the Templars' order, habit and name for ever.
changes.new: In 1312 Pope Clement V did away with the Templars' order, habit and name for ever. The Council of Vienne approved.
changes.facts_check: 1312; Clement V suppressed Templars' order, habit, name in perpetuity with Vienne's approval; split only (old FK 10.02); all kept.
